extracted.intended_audience: immigration practitioners, advocates, regulated stakeholders, and public commenters on DHS rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory/legal standards for determining whether an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge, including statutory factors, case law framing (totality of circumstances), treatment of affidavits of support and bonds, exemptions, and how receipt of various public benefits (per PRWORA) bears on determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of public charge inadmissibility (INA section 212(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 212(a)(4) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(4), provides that an alien applicant for a visa, admission, or adjustment of status is inadmissible if he or she is likely at any time to become a public charge. The public charge ground applies to any alien applying for a visa to come to the United States temporarily or permanently, for admission, or for adjustment of status to that of a lawful permanent resident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 212(a)(4) does not directly apply to applications for extension of stay or change of status because extension of stay and change of status applications are not applications for a visa, admission, or adjustment of status. Consular officers and immigration officers enforce this ground when the alien is an applicant for admission, visa, or adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum statutory factors to consider in public charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining if an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge, consular officers and immigration officers must, at a minimum, consider the alien’s age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills (INA section 212(a)(4)(B)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five enumerated factors are the statutory baseline; adjudicators must consider them in making public charge determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Public charge determinations are a prediction based upon the totality of the alien’s circumstances at the time he or she applies for an immigrant visa or admission to the United States; no single factor may be the sole criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Matter of Martinez-Lopez; Matter of Perez; Matter of Harutunian) establishes that receipt of welfare alone does not by itself establish that an alien is likely to become a public charge. Relevant considerations include mental/physical disability, advanced age, lack of funds for self-support, lack of persons in the U.S. willing/able to assist, work history, and other facts showing a likely burden on the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective evaluation elements (8 CFR 245a.3 standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory precedent holds that public charge determinations are prospective evaluations based on the alien’s age, health, income, and vocation (8 CFR 245a.3(g)(4)(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence or absence of a particular factor can never be the sole criterion. The regulation also contemplates consideration of consistent employment, income relative to poverty level, and past receipt of public cash assistance as a significant but not necessarily dispositive factor when viewed with other evidence such as employment history and capacity to earn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of affidavit of support under section 213A
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 212(a)(4) permits the consular officer or the immigration officer to consider any affidavit of support submitted under section 213A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1183a, on the applicant’s behalf when determining whether the applicant may become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When required, the applicant must submit an Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A (Form I-864). With limited exceptions, family-based immigrant visa and adjustment applicants (and some employment-based applicants) must have a sufficient affidavit of support or will be found inadmissible as likely to become a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bonds as discretionary remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien whom DHS has determined to be inadmissible on public charge grounds may, if otherwise admissible, be admitted at the Secretary’s discretion upon giving a suitable and proper bond or undertaking approved by the Secretary (purpose: ensure the alien will not become a public charge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since enactment of enforceable affidavits of support, use of public charge bonds has decreased and USCIS does not currently have a public charge bond process; the proposed rule would outline a process under which USCIS could offer public charge bonds in its discretion to applicants for adjustment of status inadmissible only on public charge grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories exempt from public charge inadmissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some immigrant and nonimmigrant categories are exempt from the public charge inadmissibility ground; DHS proposes to list these categories in regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples noted in the text include refugees, asylees, certain trafficking victims (T nonimmigrants), certain parolees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, and others statutorily identified as eligible for benefits or otherwise exempt. A lawful permanent resident typically is not an applicant for admission and thus generally not subject to 212(a)(4), except in limited statutory situations (e.g., 101(a)(13)(C)). The rule proposes to enumerate exemptions and waiver-eligible applicants (see proposed 8 CFR 212.23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to apply for waiver of public charge ground
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to list in the regulation the applicants that the law permits to apply for a waiver of the public charge inadmissibility ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory text will specify which categories may seek waivers; waiver availability and standards derive from statute and DHS discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRWORA definition of Federal public benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: PRWORA broadly defines 'Federal public benefit' to include (A) any grant, contract, loan, professional license, or commercial license provided by an agency of the United States or by appropriated funds of the United States; and (B) any retirement, welfare, health, disability, public or assisted housing, postsecondary education, food assistance, unemployment benefit, or any other similar benefit for which payments or assistance are provided to an individual, household, or family eligibility unit by an agency of the United States or by appropriated funds of the United States (8 U.S.C. 1611(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRWORA also specifies exclusions from this definition, e.g., professional or commercial licenses tied to nonimmigrant employment visas, benefits payable under reciprocal treaty agreements, and professional licenses issued to foreign nationals not physically present in the U.S. See statutory text for enumerated exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRWORA benefit-category framework (Specified, Designated, Federal Means-Tested Benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRWORA categorizes benefits as Specified Federal Programs, Designated Federal Programs, and Federal Means-Tested Benefits, with differing eligibility rules for aliens and qualified aliens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule summarizes these categories and the statutory citations governing who is eligible for each category and when (e.g., some categories permit immediate eligibility for refugees/asylees; others require 5- or 7-year residence or specific qualifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified alien classification and timing for federal means-tested benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under PRWORA, 'qualified aliens' are generally eligible for federal means-tested benefits after 5 years, and states may determine eligibility for designated federal programs; certain categories are immediately eligible (refugees, asylees, certain parolees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, Amerasians, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule provides a table of immigration categories that are 'qualified aliens' and specifies exceptions and immediate-eligibility categories; statutory citations (8 U.S.C. 1612, 1613, 1641, etc.) govern details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandfathering and program-specific exemptions (SSI and SNAP examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain beneficiaries are grandfathered or exempt from PRWORA restrictions—for example, aliens receiving SSI or SNAP on August 22, 1996 may have continued eligibility under specified conditions; SNAP-specific exemptions include children under 18 and certain tribe members and elderly aliens lawfully residing on Aug 22, 1996.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists statutory provisions and narrow exceptions (including extensions for SSI through fiscal year 2011 in some cases) and special tribal/age-based SNAP exemptions; adjudicators should consult the statutory provisions for precise applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of benefits excluded from restriction (emergency and public health benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress chose not to restrict eligibility for certain benefits, including emergency medical assistance; short-term, in-kind, non-cash emergency disaster relief; and public health assistance related to immunizations and treatment of symptoms of communicable disease (8 U.S.C. 1611(b)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule reiterates statutory carve-outs and references agency guidance (e.g., Final Specification of Community Programs Necessary For Protection Of Life Or Safety) that identify community-level in-kind services and other emergency assistance programs as exceptions to restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated Federal Programs: state discretion and time-limited eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Designated Federal Programs are programs for which states may determine eligibility for qualified aliens, and certain categories (e.g., lawful permanent residents with 40 Social Security quarters, veterans, American Indians born in Canada or tribal members) are eligible without time limit; other categories (e.g., refugees, asylees) are eligible for some programs within the first 7 years or 5 years depending on program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule provides examples (Medicaid, TANF, Social Services Block Grants) and notes that states may enact legislation to provide benefits to aliens not lawfully present; it also notes that a state choosing the federal 'qualified alien' definition is considered to have chosen the least restrictive means for federal policy purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Means-Tested Benefits: agency definitions and all-aliens exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: PRWORA contains no statutory definition for 'Federal Means-Tested Benefits' but agencies have defined covered benefits; some programs are made available to all aliens (e.g., emergency medical assistance, short-term non-cash disaster relief, National School Lunch, Child Nutrition, Head Start, certain student assistance, foster care/adoption payments, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule lists categories of programs typically treated as means-tested and lists statutory and agency citations; it also enumerates categories of aliens eligible for means-tested benefits (refugees, asylees, certain veterans, Amerasians, tribal members, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior receipt of public cash assistance as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior receipt of public cash assistance is a significant factor in public charge determinations but is not dispositive and must be weighed within the totality of circumstances and alongside employment history and other evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: INS/administrative precedent treated past receipt as relevant evidence in a prospective test (see Matter of A- and 8 CFR 245a.3 provisions). Adjudicators should not treat past welfare receipt as sole proof of likely future use of public benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory examples and cross-references to other laws and policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule cross-references numerous statutes, regulations, and administrative decisions that shape public charge analysis (e.g., INA sections, PRWORA, IIRIRA, 8 CFR provisions, Matter of decisions, and program statutes like the Social Security Act, Food Stamp Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators, practitioners, and commenters should consider the interplay of these statutes/regulations/case law when applying the public charge criteria; the rule includes tables and statutory citations for precise legal references.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and local public benefits: definitions and state-level discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: PRWORA defined 'State or local public benefit' broadly and, with certain exceptions, limited aliens' ability to obtain State and local public benefits; states may choose to provide benefits to certain aliens not lawfully present or align with the federal 'qualified alien' definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule notes that states can enact laws to extend benefits and provides references to HHS analyses of state practices; eligibility for state/local benefits may differ from federal program eligibility and can affect consideration in public charge contexts.
